1.pericope_label: And I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvellous, seven angels having the seven last plagues; for in them is filled up the wrath of God. And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name, stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God.

schools.summary: Gill treats the sign and refuses the baptismal reading of the sea. The chapter, he says, is a preparation to the pouring out of the seven vials, as other passages are to the seven epistles and the seven seals and trumpets; the vision is called a sign because what was seen was significative of future events, a sign of the coming of Christ, of his kingdom, and of the destruction of antichrist. It is a sign in heaven, where John was called up and where he had his visions, and it is another, different from that which represented the downfall of paganism, this representing the downfall of popery; it is very great, being expressive of great things such as the fall of Babylon and the great glory of the church and kingdom of Christ, and it is marvellous, for the two grand events it respects are very wonderful, that antichrist, once in such power, should be destroyed, and that by such weak means in the esteem of men as the preaching of the Gospel. On the sea of glass Gill begins by denying that baptism is meant, and offers rather the blood of Christ, which may be compared to a sea for its abundant virtue and efficacy in cleansing from all sin, and to a sea of glass since in it are clearly seen free justification, full pardon, peace and reconciliation, and which may be said to be mingled with fire, being attended in the application of it with the Spirit of God, whose gifts and graces are sometimes signified by fire. According to others, he adds, the sea may represent the pure church of God as washed in the blood of the Lamb, compared to a sea for the multitude of which it consists, and to a sea of glass because of the transparency of its principles and practices, and mingled with the fire of love and zeal; but most interpreters, Gill reports, understand it of the world, which is like a sea for the multitude of its inhabitants and sometimes like a troubled one because of the restlessness of the wicked in it, though here it is like a sea of glass for its quiet.

Henry describes the preparation of matters for the pouring out of the seven vials, committed to seven angels, and observes how these angels appeared to the apostle in heaven, in a wonderful manner, on account of the work they had to do, which was to finish the destruction of antichrist, God being now about to pour out his seven last plagues upon that interest so that, the measure of Babylon's sins being filled up, they should now find the full measure of his vindictive wrath; and on account of the spectators and witnesses of their commission, all that had gotten the victory over the beast. These stood on a sea of glass, representing this world, as some think, a brittle thing that shall be broken to pieces; or, as others, the gospel covenant, alluding to the brazen sea in the temple in which the priests were to wash, the faithful servants of God standing upon the foundation of the righteousness of Christ; or, as others, the Red Sea, that stood as it were congealed while the Israelites went through, the pillar of fire reflecting light upon the waters so that they would seem to have fire mingled with them, showing that the fire of God's wrath against Pharaoh and his horses should dissolve the congealed waters and destroy them thereby, to which there seems to be an allusion in their singing the song of Moses. In that song, Henry notes, they extol the greatness of God's works and the justice and truth of his ways, both in delivering his people and destroying their enemies, rejoicing in hope and in the near prospect they had of this, though it was not yet accomplished; and they call upon all nations to render unto God the glory due.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson set out the vision and the words. Barnes gives the chapter's connexion with the previous one, in which pledges had been given that all the enemies of religion would be cut off and the church ultimately triumphant, and particularly that the Antichristian power represented by the beast would be destroyed; this chapter commences the statement of the manner in which those pledges would be accomplished. The seven angels appear with the seven last plagues that fill up or complete the wrath of God, representing the wrath to come upon the beast; those who in former times had gotten the victory over the beast appear standing on a sea of glass, rejoicing and rendering thanks for the assurance that this great enemy of the church was now to be destroyed. On the sea Barnes compares the earlier vision, where it was entirely clear and pellucid because the emblem was designed to represent the pure worship of heaven; here a portion is red like fire, so that it is not wholly clear but a tesselated expanse, and the idea of punishment on the foes of God is united with it. If it is proper to suggest the meaning from conjecture, he says, it would be that the foundation and main element of all the divine dealings is justice or holiness, represented by the portion that seemed to be glass, with the image of wrath or anger intermingled, represented by the portion that was fiery, so that the very sight of the pavement on which they stood when worshipping God would keep impressive views of his character and dealings before their minds. Ellicott notes that the sign is a token and not a mere empty wonder, that it introduces a new set of scenes in which the same characters reappear, and that the seer sees seven angels, not the seven angels, so that it is perfectly needless to ask what angels they are or to try to identify them with the trumpet angels. The statement that these are the last plagues seems to him to show that the set of visions now commencing carries us down to the end of the age, there being no other plagues after these, so that the vials, like the seals and the trumpets, run up to the final consummation. They are called plagues, he adds, and the word carries us back to Egypt, on which fell the ten plagues that showed forth God's righteous power and exposed the hollow pretensions of the magicians and their gods; in like manner the plagues of God fall upon the wild beast-power of later ages, and they are plagues because they are sent forth not, like the trumpets, to warn men to repent, but upon those who have obstinately refused to return, being not goads to the wavering but strokes upon the wilful and hardened and directed against those who are deliberately hostile. On the sea of glass Ellicott sets the vision against its opposites: the wild beast rose out of the sea and the evil-hearted woman sits upon many waters, both drawing strength from the wild and ungoverned impulses of human passion, whereas near the throne of God is the calm and translucent sea of God's counsels of righteousness and love, now clear as crystal, now ruddy with the fire of righteous indignation, the expression of his eternal will against sin. Those who are victorious he describes literally as those who conquer out of the wild beast, coming off conquerors out of the struggle and escaping victorious from his image and from his mark; when the seer sees them they are standing upon the shore of the sea of glass, holding harps of God, which are called God's not merely because they are dedicated to him but because they are truly his, since the life which has been a discord to the world rises into true music before God, and those who will make their life a melody must take it first as a conflict. Robertson observes that the sign looks back to the earlier chapter after the intervening series, that the Seven Bowls are parallel with the Seven Seals and the Seven Trumpets though with an even closer connection to the preceding chapters, which Swete calls the drama of the long conflict between the church and the world. The adjective rendered marvellous is an old verbal one from the verb to wonder; the wonder extends to the end of this vision; the number seven seems particularly appropriate for finality and completeness; and the verb rendered is finished is a proleptic prophetic aorist. On the sea he notes that the item about its being mingled with fire is not in the earlier vision, which was a vision of peace, but here adds to the splendour, and that this parenthesis gives a picture of the martyrs in their state of bliss; the harps of God are an objective genitive, for the worship of God.

Clarke and Wesley take the structure and the sequel. Clarke observes that God's judgments on the enemies of his Church have already been pointed out under the emblems of harvest and vintage, but are further signified by the seven vials, which are called the seven last plagues of God; these appear to fall under the seventh and last trumpet, for as the seventh seal contained the seven trumpets, so the seventh trumpet contains the seven vials, and as seven angels sounded the seven trumpets, so seven angels are appointed to pour out the seven vials, angels being always the ministers of Providence. This chapter, he says, contains the opening vision which is preparatory to the pouring out of the vials. He adds that the Targum of Jonathan on Isaiah uses the same words employed by the evangelist here, rendering the cup of the Lord's fury as the phials of the cup of malediction, and again the cup of malediction as the phials of the cup of his indignation. On the sea of glass Clarke describes a spacious lucid plain around the throne, from which fiery coruscations were continually emitted, or else the reflection of the light upon this lucid plain producing the prismatic colours of the most vivid rainbow. Wesley notes that the angels had the plagues before they had the phials, which were the instruments whereby those plagues were to be conveyed, and that they are termed the last because by them the wrath of God is fulfilled hitherto: God had borne his enemies with much longsuffering, but now his wrath goes forth to the uttermost, pouring plagues on the earth from one end to the other and round its whole circumference; yet even after these plagues, he adds, the holy wrath of God against his other enemies does not cease. On the sea he says it was before clear as crystal but is now mingled with fire, which devours the adversaries; that those who gained, or were gaining, the victory over the wild beast are more of whom were yet to come; that the mark of the beast, the mark of his name and the number of his name seem to mean here nearly the same thing; and that the harps of God were given by him and appropriated to his praise. The song, he observes, was sung while the angels were coming out with their plagues, who are therefore mentioned both before and after it.

Victorinus of Pettau and Bede expound the sign. Victorinus says that the wrath of God always strikes the obstinate people with seven plagues, that is perfectly, as it is said in Leviticus, and that these shall be in the last time, when the Church shall have gone out of the midst; on the second verse he says that those standing upon the sea of glass with harps stood steadfastly in the faith upon their baptism, and having their confession in their mouth shall exult in the kingdom before God. Bede observes that the order is renewed here, and that, as if about to relate the same plagues of the last persecution, the writer wished the hearer to be made attentive by calling it a sign great and marvellous. The seven he takes to mean the Church, which is replete with sevenfold grace; they are called the last because in them the wrath of God is consummated, for the wrath of God ever smites the rebellious people with seven plagues, as he says repeatedly in Leviticus, I will smite you with seven plagues, and these are to be the last when the Church shall have come forth from the midst of it. The glass he takes for the pellucid fount of Baptism, which is consecrated by the fire of the Holy Ghost, or else because it pertains to the nature of fire in that it is made red by martyrdom; they who overcome the wiles of the beast appear in consequence to stand upon a baptism of fire, since they desire, as the Apostle says, to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered unto the saints. The harps he takes to mean that they have the hearts of those who praise dedicated to God, and melodious with the truth of both Testaments, or else the flesh extended on the wood of passion; and here not the sound of the voice alone is signified but the iteration of a good work. Of the song he says he has found it in both Testaments, where the Lord, both true and merciful, is celebrated as the Judge who is to be worshipped by all ages; and of the temple, that the writer repeats what he had set forth before, the vision according with the song.

debates: What the sea of glass is. Bede and Victorinus both take it for baptism, Bede adding that it is made red by martyrdom so that the victors stand upon a baptism of fire; Gill opens by refusing that reading and offers the blood of Christ, then the church washed in it, and reports that most interpreters understand the world; Henry lists the world, the gospel covenant and the Red Sea without choosing; Ellicott makes it the calm sea of God's counsels, set against the sea from which the beast rose; Barnes conjectures justice figured by the glass and wrath by the fire; Clarke declines symbolism for a lucid plain emitting fiery coruscations.

How the vials stand to the seals and trumpets. Clarke nests them, the seventh seal containing the trumpets and the seventh trumpet the vials; Robertson sets the three series parallel, with a closer connection to the chapters just before; Ellicott argues from the word last that the vials, like the seals and trumpets, run up to the final consummation.

What the seven signifies. Victorinus and Bede both take it of perfection, citing the sevenfold plagues of Leviticus; Bede further identifies the seven angels with the Church, replete with sevenfold grace; Robertson takes the number as appropriate to finality; Ellicott insists the text says seven angels and not the seven, so that identifying them is needless.

Whether the wrath here is the last. Ellicott holds that there are no plagues after these and that the series runs to the end of the age; Wesley grants that God's wrath now goes forth to the uttermost but denies that it ceases afterwards against his other enemies; Gill and Henry keep the reference to the destruction of antichrist rather than to a final judgment.
outliers: Bede alone reads the seven angels as the Church itself, replete with sevenfold grace, where every other witness takes them for angelic ministers of the plagues.
Clarke alone supports the word for the vials from the Targum of Jonathan, which renders the cup of the Lord's fury in Isaiah by the same term the evangelist uses here.
themes: filled up the wrath of God
a sea of glass mingled with fire
gotten the victory over the beast

3.pericope_label: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints. Who shall not fear thee, O Lord, and glorify thy name? for thou only art holy: for all nations shall come and worship before thee; for thy judgments are made manifest.

schools.summary: Gill takes the song for one like that of Moses rather than the same, offering two senses: either that they observed the law of Moses, which he as a servant in the Lord's house faithfully delivered, keeping it distinct from the Gospel and not blending the two as in former times; or rather that they sang a song like that of Moses, and on a like occasion. Pharaoh, he says, was the very picture of the pope of Rome, his oppression and cruel usage of the Israelites representing the tyranny and cruelty of the Romish antichrist, while the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt and the destruction of the Egyptians at the Red Sea, which occasioned the song of Moses, were an emblem of God's bringing his people out of antichristian bondage and of the ruin of antichrist, upon which this song is sung; and Rome, he notes, is called Egypt in this book. The Jews, Gill adds, have a notion that the very song of Moses itself will be sung in the world to come, in the days of the Messiah, since they say there are in it the times of the Messiah. On the next verse he applies the promise: at this time the people of the Jews shall seek after Christ and fear him and his goodness, the forces of the Gentiles shall be brought into Zion, whose heart shall then fear and be enlarged, and the fear of the Lord will be in all places and in all men, both Jews and Gentiles.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle the song and its words. Barnes calls it a song of thanksgiving and praise such as Moses taught the Hebrew people to sing after their deliverance from Egyptian bondage, and says the meaning is not that they would sing that identical song, but that as Moses taught the people to celebrate their deliverance with an appropriate hymn of praise, the redeemed would celebrate their redemption in a similar manner; there is an obvious propriety in referring to the song of Moses, since the circumstances are very similar and the occasion of the redemption from that formidable Antichristian power had a strong resemblance to the rescue from Egyptian bondage. The song of the Lamb is the hymn sung in honour of the Lamb as their great deliverer. Great and marvellous means that great power was evinced in redeeming them and that the interposition of the divine goodness was such as to excite wonder and admiration, while Lord God Almighty seems to Barnes to mean the same as the phrase so common in the Old Testament, Jehovah, God of hosts, the union of the appellations giving solemnity to the ascription of praise. On the next verse he takes fear in the sense the Scriptures commonly give it when applied to God, of reverence and adoration, with perhaps some idea of awe included, since the judgments about to be inflicted on the beast and his image should teach men to reverence God and to honour him as Ruler of the earth. When it is said that he only is holy, Barnes says the expression is used in a comparative sense: he is so pure that in comparison with him no one else is holy. That all nations shall come and worship follows from the punishments inflicted on this Antichristian power, and Barnes notes that everywhere in the New Testament the destruction of that power is connected with the promise of the speedy conversion of the world. Ellicott observes that they join their voices to the music of their harps, and that the song of Moses was a paean of victory over Pharaoh and his hosts: Israel stood on the margin of the Red Sea and saw the tokens of the overthrow of the great world-power of that day, and so these saints stand by the border of the fire-blent sea of glass and sing the song of triumph over the doom of the great world-powers of every age, the cases being parallel and the songs alike. It would not be out of place, he adds, were the words of that other song of Moses, the man of God, to be heard from those who are made glad according to the days of their affliction and clothed with the beauty of the Lord their God. They also sing the song of the Lamb, for the Apocalypse is full of Christ, the Lamb being the axis on which the world of its scenery moves and the key of earth's history, since the victory of the saints is in him and their song of triumph is of him who put a new song in their mouth. On the next verse Ellicott would render it, Who will not fear, omitting the word Thee, and notes that the word rendered holy is not that which is usually employed when the holiness of God is spoken of; it is a word which, when applied to men, denotes one who reverences the sacred obligations of natural and moral order, apart from the thought of mere law or custom, and which is applied here to God to denote the recognition of those sacred obligations which the character of God imposes upon himself. It is the remembrance that God will, as Judge of all the earth, do right, and will vindicate the expectations of those who stay themselves upon his character, which generates a holy fear of him. The last clause he would translate, All the nations worship, because Thy judgments are manifested, and adds that the song is one in anticipation: the angels of judgment are going forth and the righteous dealings of God will be seen, but these things are spoken of as though accomplished, their completion being a divine certainty. Robertson calls it a song of victory like that of Moses after crossing the Red Sea, and the song of the Lamb a separate note of victory, though one song and not two; Charles, he reports, finds it impossible to reconcile the two expressions if genuine, but Robertson calls that a needless objection. The words, he shows, come from the Old Testament: great from one psalm, wonderful from another, the title Lord God the Almighty from Amos, righteous and true from Deuteronomy, and the address to the King of the ages from a form like that in Jeremiah, while some manuscripts read the king of the saints and some the king of the nations; John thus combines in Hebraic tone the expressions of the old and the new in the song to the Glorified Messiah. On the next verse he notes the rhetorical question with a double negative, the change from aorist subjunctive to future indicative, and the predicate adjectives meaning that God is alone holy, being alone perfectly holy; the verbs for coming and worshipping are drawn from a psalm, and the last verb is a prophetic aorist. This martyr's song, Robertson concludes, has the ring of great poetry.

Clarke and Wesley take the song's identity and its shape. Clarke says they sing the song of Moses, that which Moses sang when he and the Israelites, by the miraculous power of God, had got safely through the Red Sea and saw their enemies all destroyed, and that the song of the Lamb is the same song adapted to the state of the suffering but now delivered Christians. God's works, he says, are descriptive of his infinite power and wisdom, and the title Lord God Almighty is nearly the same as Jehovah, God of hosts; every step God takes in grace or providence is according to justice, and he carefully accomplishes all his threatenings and all his promises, to which he is bound by his truth. On the next verse Clarke says that all should fear and worship this true God because he is just and true and holy, that his saints should love and obey him because he is their King, and that they and all men should acknowledge his judgments because they are made manifest. Wesley says the song is so called partly from its near agreement with the words of that song which Moses sang after passing the Red Sea, and of that which he taught the children of Israel a little before his death, but chiefly because Moses was the minister and representative of the Jewish church as Christ is of the church universal, which is why it is also termed the song of the Lamb. It consists, he says, of six parts which answer each other: great and wonderful are thy works, Lord God Almighty, for thou only art gracious; just and true are thy ways, O King of the nations, for all the nations shall come and worship before thee; who would not fear thee, O Lord, and glorify thy name, for thy judgments are made manifest. We know and acknowledge, Wesley paraphrases, that all thy works in and toward all the creatures are great and wonderful, and that thy ways with all the children of men, good and evil, are just and true; and this grace is the spring of all those wonderful works, even of his destroying the enemies of his people, as in the psalm the clause about mercy enduring for ever is subjoined to the thanksgiving for works of vengeance as well as for the delivering of the righteous. That all the nations shall come and worship before thee means that they shall serve him as their king with joyful reverence.

debates: Whether the song is the song of Moses or one like it. Clarke identifies it with what Moses sang at the Red Sea, adapted to Christians; Barnes denies the identity and asserts only a likeness of occasion and manner; Gill allows either that they kept the law Moses delivered or, rather, that they sang a song like his; Wesley finds two songs of Moses behind the phrase and rests the name chiefly on Moses's representative office.

Whether one song is meant or two. Robertson calls the song of the Lamb a separate note of victory and yet insists on one song, reporting and dismissing the objection that the two expressions cannot be reconciled; Ellicott keeps them parallel rather than identical, and suggests that a third song of Moses, the psalm of the man of God, would suit the occasion.

What the word rendered holy means. Barnes takes the clause comparatively, that in comparison with God no one else is holy, and Robertson renders it that he is alone holy; Ellicott points out that the word is not the one ordinarily used of God's holiness, and takes it of God's recognition of the obligations his own character imposes on him, so that the fear it generates rests on the certainty that the Judge of all the earth will do right.

Whether the song looks back or forward. Ellicott alone marks the tense, calling the song one of anticipation, since the angels of judgment are only now going forth while the words speak as though all were accomplished; Barnes and Gill both read the promise of the nations' worship as the sequel of the judgments, Barnes connecting it with the New Testament's general expectation of a speedy conversion of the world.
outliers: Wesley alone treats the song as a composition to be analysed, laying it out in six parts that answer one another in pairs, the works matched by grace, the ways by the coming of the nations, and the question of fear by the manifest judgments.

Ellicott alone rests his reading of the divine holiness on the choice of an unusual word, distinguishing it from the term normally used of God and drawing from it the sense of obligations that God's character lays upon himself.
themes: the song of Moses the servant of God
great and marvellous are thy works
just and true are thy ways
all nations shall come and worship

5.pericope_label: And after that I looked, and, behold, the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony in heaven was opened: And the seven angels came out of the temple, having the seven plagues, clothed in pure and white linen, and having their breasts girded with golden girdles.

schools.summary: Gill notes that after John had seen the previous vision he looked again and saw what follows, and that by the seven angels coming out of the temple it appears that they are such as belong to the church of Christ, being either ministers or members of churches, who will be the executioners of God's wrath upon the beast and his followers; he observes that some copies, and the Complutensian edition, read out of heaven instead.

Henry observes how these angels appeared, coming out of heaven to execute their commission when the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony in heaven was opened, and finds here an allusion to the holiest of all in the tabernacle and temple, where was the mercy-seat covering the ark of the testimony, where the high priest made intercession and God communed with his people and heard their prayers. By this, as it is here mentioned, he says four things may be understood: that in the judgments God was now about to execute upon the antichristian interest he was fulfilling the prophecies and promises of his word and covenant, which were there always before him and of which he was ever mindful; that in this work he was answering the prayers of the people, which were offered to him by their great high priest; that he was herein avenging the quarrel of his own Son and our Saviour Jesus Christ, whose offices and authority had been usurped, his name dishonoured, and the great designs of his death opposed, by antichrist and his adherents; and that he was opening a wider door of liberty for his people to worship him in numerous solemn assemblies, without the fear of their enemies. On their array Henry notes that they were clothed with pure and white linen and had their breasts girded with golden girdles, which was the habit of the high priests when they went in to enquire of God.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson identify the temple and describe the angels. Barnes says that after seeing the redeemed celebrating the praises of God, the writer saw the preparation made for executing these purposes of judgment; the word tabernacle means properly a booth, hut or tent, and was the name commonly given to the tent erected in the wilderness for the service of God, the same word coming naturally to be applied to the temple reared for the same purpose in Jerusalem. It is called the tabernacle of testimony because it was a testimony or witness of the presence of God among the people, serving to keep up the remembrance of him; and the word temple here does not refer to the whole of the building called the temple but to the holy of holies, regarded as the peculiar dwelling-place of God, so that it was this sacred place, usually closed from all access, that now seemed to be opened, implying that the command to execute these purposes came directly from God himself. Of the angels Barnes says each one was entrusted with a single plague to be executed upon the earth, the symbols of their office being given them afterwards; their clothing in pure and white linen is the emblem of holiness, the common representation in regard to the heavenly inhabitants, and the golden girdles mean that they were attired in a manner befitting their rank and condition. Ellicott would render the opening, And after these things I saw, and there was opened the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony in the heaven; the expression sounds cumbrous, he grants, but is nevertheless suitable, since Stephen spoke of the tabernacle of witness in the wilderness, which was made after the pattern showed in the mount, and the tabernacle was well called the tabernacle of witness, for it contained the ark of the testimony with the Law of God and was a perpetual witness of God's presence among his people. The temple of the tabernacle is thus the shrine or inner sanctuary of the heavenly true tabernacle, after the pattern of which the tabernacle of Moses was fashioned, which is now opened. On the next verse he would render, And there came out the seven angels who had the seven plagues from the temple, clothed in linen, pure, glistening, and girt about their breasts with golden girdles, and notes that the temple is the inner shrine which was measured earlier and out of which the angel with the sharp sickle came for the vintage. It is well to remember this, he adds, for these plagues are not, like the judgments of the trumpet, calls to repentance; they are plagues on those who have refused to return, who have rejected the sanctuary, the tabernacle of witness which the Lord pitched among men, and who have refused, like obstinate builders, the stone which has become the head of the corner: out of the rejected temple the angels of wrath come, and it is ever true that out of rejected mercies the heaviest of plagues are forged. The angels are clad in a garb resembling that of Christ, having come forth to do his bidding and being clothed in raiment which indicates their righteous errand; and Ellicott notes that instead of linen some manuscripts have a stone, so that the angels would be clad in a stone, pure and brilliant, there being a parallel thought in Ezekiel's description of the splendour of the King of Tyre in Eden, the garden of God, where every precious stone was his covering. Robertson observes that Charles calls the phrase about the temple strange language, and judges that probably the tabernacle or tent of witness is in mind, and the tent of meeting rather than the temple in Jerusalem. On the next verse he notes the proleptic and prophetic aorist for their coming out, that the angels are those of the first verse and that the bowls are not given them until later, and that the participle rendered arrayed is a perfect passive with the accusative retained after a verb of clothing, so that the text reads with a stone pure and bright, though some manuscripts read linen; the girding is likewise a perfect passive participle, with golden girdles in the accusative.

Clarke and Wesley take the temple and the vesture. Clarke explains the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony as the temple which succeeded the tabernacle, in which was the testimony, namely the two tables, Aaron's rod, the pot of manna and the holy anointing oil, all bearing testimony to the truth of God and his miraculous interposition on their behalf. The seven angels came out of the temple, he says, to show that they were sent from God himself, and were habited as priests. Wesley calls the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony the holiest of all, and says it was opened, disclosing a new theatre for the coming forth of the judgments of God now made manifest. The angels came out as having received their instructions from the oracle of God himself, John having seen them in heaven before they went into the temple; they appeared in habits like those the high priest wore when he went into the most holy place to consult the oracle, in which was the visible testimony of God's presence. Linen, Wesley adds, is the habit of service and attendance; pure means unspotted and unsullied, while white means bright and shining, which implies much more than bare innocence; and their breasts girt with golden girdles is a token of their high dignity and glorious rest.

debates: What the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony is. Barnes and Wesley identify it with the holy of holies; Clarke reads it of the Jerusalem temple which succeeded the tabernacle and housed the testimony; Robertson prefers the wilderness tent of meeting to the temple in Jerusalem, reporting that Charles calls the phrase strange; Ellicott defends the cumbrous expression as the inner sanctuary of the heavenly true tabernacle.

What the opening signifies. Henry finds four things in it, the fulfilling of the covenant promises, the answering of the prayers of the saints, the avenging of the Son whose authority had been usurped, and a wider liberty of worship; Barnes takes it only as showing that the command came directly from God; Wesley as disclosing a new theatre of judgment; Ellicott turns it against the objects of the plagues, since it is out of the rejected sanctuary that the angels of wrath come.

Who the seven angels are. Clarke, Wesley and Barnes all take their emergence from the temple as proof that they are sent immediately from God; Gill argues from the same fact that they belong to the church of Christ and are ministers or members of churches who will execute the wrath, and notes a variant reading of out of heaven.

What their dress is and means. Robertson takes the text to read precious stone, pure and bright, with linen as the variant, while Ellicott takes linen as the text and the stone as the variant, comparing Ezekiel on the King of Tyre; Henry, Clarke and Wesley all read the vesture as priestly, Barnes as the ordinary emblem of angelic holiness, and Ellicott as resembling the garb of Christ whose bidding they go to do.
outliers: Gill alone makes the seven angels men, arguing from their coming out of the temple that they are ministers or members of churches who will be the executioners of the wrath.
Ellicott alone draws a moral from the place the angels come from, that since they issue from the sanctuary men have rejected, it is out of rejected mercies that the heaviest plagues are forged.
themes: the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony
the seven angels came out of the temple
clothed in pure and white linen
their breasts girded with golden girdles

7.pericope_label: And one of the four beasts gave unto the seven angels seven golden vials full of the wrath of God, who liveth for ever and ever. And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God, and from his power; and no man was able to enter into the temple, till the seven plagues of the seven angels were fulfilled.

schools.summary: Gill identifies the living creatures and reads the smoke. The four living creatures, he says, are the ministers of the Gospel, and this was one, or the first of them, who was like a lion for fortitude and courage and whose voice was as the noise of thunder, so that he fitly represents those ministers who shall give out the vials of God's wrath. No particular person is designed who shall be at this time, and much less Luke the evangelist, as Lord Napier thinks, nor Peter, who prophesied of the last time, as Grotius holds, but a set of Gospel ministers comparable to one of the living creatures John had before seen. On the smoke Gill denies that it is the smoke of false doctrine and superstition, which comes out of the bottomless pit, since this comes from God, and since Gospel churches will grow purer and purer while the seven angels are pouring out the vials. It may rather be understood, he says, of judicial blindness and hardness of heart upon the antichristian party, which will come upon them from God in righteous judgment, so that they will not be reformed by the plagues and vials of wrath, nor repent of their sins, but blaspheme God, who has power over the plagues, and so shall not be able to enter into the temple; or else it may design God's powerful and gracious presence in his church, in allusion to the cloud which filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter, and which filled the temple so that the priests could not minister.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson describe the vessels and the smoke. Barnes notes that which one of the four living creatures is not mentioned, and takes them, on the explanation given earlier, to symbolise the great principles of the divine government, so that in events so closely connected with the honour of God and the triumph of his cause there was a propriety in representing these living creatures as particularly interested. The word rendered vial, he says, means properly a bowl or goblet having more breadth than depth, whereas our word vial, though derived from it, means rather a thin long bottle of glass such as apothecaries use; the word would be better rendered bowl or goblet, and probably such bowls as were used in the temple service are meant. They are called elsewhere vials of the wrath of God and are here said to be full of it, the allusion seeming to be to a drinking cup filled with poison and given to persons to drink, drawn from one of the methods of punishment in ancient times, so that these vessels became emblems of divine wrath to be inflicted on the beast and his image. On the smoke Barnes calls it the usual symbol of the divine presence in the temple, and cites Sinai, which was altogether on a smoke because the Lord descended on it in fire; the purpose here seems partly to represent the smoke as the proper symbol of the divine presence and partly to represent it as so filling the temple that no one could enter until the seven plagues were fulfilled. The meaning, he judges, is that no one would be permitted to enter to make intercession and turn away his wrath, since the purpose of punishment had been formed and would certainly be executed, the agents having been sent forth and by no means to be recalled; the mercy-seat in this respect was inaccessible, the time of judgment on the great foe had come, and the destruction of the enemy of the church was certain. Ellicott would render it, And one from among the four living beings gave to the seven angels seven golden vials full of the wrath of God, and explains that the vials are the shallow bowls which were used for incense, now filled with the wrath which is to be poured out upon the kingdoms that have not called upon God's name. These vials are given by one of the living creatures who represent creation, so that it is through creation that the wrath of God can visit the rebellious, that wrath being simply the operation of God's righteous law against sin, since he has given to all things a law which cannot be broken and which is adverse to evil and will in the end root it out. On the smoke Ellicott would translate that the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his might, and that no one was able to enter until the seven plagues should be finished. As in the wilderness and at the dedication of Solomon's temple the tokens of God's presence filled the temple, so it is now, but with a difference, since it is smoke and not cloud which is the symbol of God's presence. The vision which most nearly corresponds, he judges, is that of Isaiah, where the prophet beheld the vision of God, his train filled the temple, the house was filled with smoke, and a message of judgment was given declaring that the sin of the people had reached a climax: they had trifled with convictions, and henceforward the words of God's servants would harden rather than awaken them, until the desolating judgments had fallen. The general drift of the present vision is similar: the days of warning are over, the plagues which now fall will fall on those who have trifled with convictions, and the sanctuary which was opened as a refuge is now closed, none being able to enter till the plagues have descended; the time has come when the judgments of God fail to stir the conscience which has been deadened by sin, and the day when the gracious influence towards repentance was felt has passed. Robertson calls the vessels golden saucers, not full of incense as in the earlier vision but full of the wrath of God who lives for ever and ever, and calls them portents of dreadful events. On the smoke he notes the aorist passive of the verb to fill full with the genitive, says that smoke is here the symbol of God's presence as at Sinai and in Isaiah, and calls the temporal clause a metaphorical and symbolic smoke screen to keep all out of the sanctuary for the time being.

Clarke and Wesley take the vessels and the precedents. Clarke observes on the smoke that the tabernacle was so filled when consecrated by Moses, and the temple when consecrated by Solomon, and that this account seems at least partly copied from those; and he adds that when the high priest entered into the holy of holies, and the ordinary priest into the holy place, they always carried with them a great deal of smoking incense, which filled those places with smoke and darkness, preventing them from considering too attentively the parts and ornaments of those holy places, and thus serving to produce an air of majesty in the temple which none dared to approach without the deepest reverence; to this, he notes, Calmet thinks the allusion may be here. Wesley observes that one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels the phials after they were come out of the temple, that the Greek word signifies vessels broader at the top than at the bottom, and that their being full of the wrath of God who liveth for ever and ever is a circumstance which adds greatly to the dreadfulness of his wrath. On the smoke he says the cloud of glory was the visible manifestation of God's presence in the tabernacle and temple, and was a sign of protection at the erecting of the tabernacle and at the dedication of the temple; but in the judgment of Korah the glory of the Lord appeared when he and his companions were swallowed up by the earth, so that the emblem of smoke from the glory of God is as proper to express the execution of judgment as to be a sign of favour, both proceeding from the power of God and in both of which he is glorified. None, he adds, not even of those who ordinarily stood before God, could go into the inmost part of the temple till the seven plagues of the seven angels were fulfilled, which did not take up a long time like the seven trumpets but swiftly followed each other.

debates: Who the four living creatures are. Gill makes them the ministers of the Gospel and rejects by name the identification of this one with Luke, which he ascribes to Lord Napier, and with Peter, which he ascribes to Grotius; Barnes takes them for the great principles of the divine government; Ellicott takes them for creation itself, so that the wrath reaches the rebellious through the created order.

What the vessels are. Barnes objects that the English word vial suggests a narrow glass bottle whereas the Greek means a broad bowl or goblet, and finds the image in the ancient punishment of a poisoned cup; Wesley agrees on the shape; Ellicott and Robertson identify them by their ordinary use as the shallow saucers of incense, now filled with wrath instead.

What the smoke signifies. Barnes and Robertson take it as the ordinary symbol of the divine presence, Robertson calling it a smoke screen that keeps all out for the time; Clarke treats the account as partly copied from the consecrations of tabernacle and temple, and adds the priest's incense as a second explanation; Wesley sets the same emblem on both sides, a sign of favour at the dedications and of judgment in the case of Korah; Ellicott finds the true parallel in Isaiah's vision and makes the smoke a token of hardening; Gill offers judicial blindness on the antichristian party or else God's gracious presence in his church.

Why none could enter. Barnes says none would be permitted to enter and make intercession, the purpose of punishment being fixed and the mercy-seat for the time inaccessible; Ellicott says the day of gracious influence towards repentance has passed and the refuge is closed; Wesley notes that not even those who ordinarily stood before God could go in, and that these plagues followed one another swiftly, unlike the trumpets.
outliers: Gill alone treats the living creatures as men, making them ministers of the Gospel and naming two earlier identifications of this one with an individual apostle or evangelist in order to reject both.

Wesley alone shows the same emblem doing opposite work, since the glory that protected at the dedication of tabernacle and temple was the glory that appeared when Korah was swallowed up, so that smoke may signify favour or judgment indifferently.
